newsitem.title: USA: American, British air link seen pushing fares higher.
newsitem.headline: American, British air link seen pushing fares higher.

text.p: Airfares between the United States and Britain could soar as American Airlines and British Airways form an alliance, unless many more landing slots are opened at London's Heathrow airport, a study released Tuesday showed.
At the same time, U.S. and British officials resumed talks in Washington on a free-market "open skies" agreement that would include opening Heathrow to more U.S. flights.

The Consumer Federation of America said the alliance, proposed last year by the two big airlines, could cost travelers more than $500 million a year in higher fares, raising the cost of tickets by 20 percent to 40 percent.
The study called for American and BA to divest themselves of 560 to 840 slots a week at London Heathrow airport, about 25 percent of their holdings, to open the popular airport to competing airlines.

Britain's Office of Fair Trading has proposed that British Airways free 168 of its Heathrow slots a week to allow rivals to serve the airport, considered a key transfer point for flights beyond Britain to Continental Europe.

The U.S. Department of Transportation has said it would not approve the alliance, and the required antitrust immunity, unless a free market air accord was first signed that included a major opening of Heathrow slots to other U.S. carriers.
The "open skies" talks now being held have been conducted off and on over the past two years, with U.S. demands that Britain giving up Heathrow slots a major stumbling block.
There was no indication an agreement would be reached during the current round of negotiations.
American and British Airways have argued their link would increase competition because the "open skies" accord that would precede it would allow many additional U.S. flights to Heathrow.

Mark Cooper, the Consumer Federation's research director, said if only a few slots were relinquished, they could end up with only a handful of U.S. carriers with their own "fortress airports" in the United States, which they would dominate.

With only a few new slots, he said, Northwest Airlines could dominate Detroit for flights to Heathrow, Delta Air Lines could dominate Atlanta and USAir Philadelphia, and these "fortresses" would enable carriers to increase fares.
"We would like the administration to take a hard look at this market," Cooper said, calling for public hearings.
"Where competition exists, consumers get good prices," Cooper said. "Where it doesn't, they don't."

But American spokesman Chris Chiames said the supply of slots would increase as American and British Airways ceded slots as planned. "I have to worry about any group that says 'when supply goes up, prices will go up, too,'" he said.

He added that he wondered how well the group understood airline economics when it questioned the impact on competition of the American-British Airways alliance but did not question the bigger marketing link-up last year of United Airlines and Lufthansa.
